Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.

Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democrats in the state Legislature placed Proposition 2 on the November ballot to give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.
The limit applies to most other appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the “rainy day” fund and other reserves.
California voters also have capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund at 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short-term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
In effect, the measure would allow the governor and the Legislature to put more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid triggering rebates.
Advertisement
For example, if the spending limit is $400 billion for the year, and revenue hits $410 billion, the measure would give lawmakers the option to deposit the $10 billion above the spending limit into the rainy day fund, direct the money to infrastructure or give it to local governments, instead of returning the funding to taxpayers and increasing funding for schools.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Newsom, legislative Democrats and the California Democratic Party say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during a recession or stock market crash.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Reform California, a political action committee started by state Sen. Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), and legislative Republicans argue the proposal will allow Democrats to spend more money and hold on to revenue that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for deposits into a savings account to count as spending under state law.
California’s budget revenue also is vulnerable to dramatic and at times unpredictable swings from year to year based on stock market activity. Newsom has said the state should have more flexibility during times of surplus to deposit money into the reserve accounts that lawmakers could then use during deficits to prevent big cuts to social services.
Advertisement
Statewide voters originally adopted the constitutional spending limit during an antitax wave in the late 1970s. Subsequent changes weakened the measure with exemptions to the limit for different kinds of appropriations, such as spending on infrastructure, and made it easier for lawmakers to avoid exceeding the limit and triggering rebates.
Revenue last exceeded the Gann Limit in 2021 when the pandemic left California with a predicted tax surplus of about $75 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-10/gavin-newsom-new-stimulus-checks-californians-rent-assistance). As he campaigned against a failed recall, the governor set aside about $11.8 billion in cash rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election) for middle class and low-income residents under a program he called the “Golden State Stimulus.” The Newsom administration predicted a historic surplus of nearly $100 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-05-13/california-budget-surplus-swells-to-97-billion-under-newsom-new-plan) the next year.

Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher.

Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher.

The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democrats in the state Legislature placed Proposition 2 on the November ballot to give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.

Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher.

Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democrats in the state Legislature placed Proposition 2 on the November ballot to give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.
The limit applies to most other appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the “rainy day” fund and other reserves.
California voters also have capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund at 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short-term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
In effect, the measure would allow the governor and the Legislature to put more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid triggering rebates.
Advertisement
For example, if the spending limit is $400 billion for the year, and revenue hits $410 billion, the measure would give lawmakers the option to deposit the $10 billion above the spending limit into the rainy day fund, direct the money to infrastructure or give it to local governments, instead of returning the funding to taxpayers and increasing funding for schools.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Newsom, legislative Democrats and the California Democratic Party say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during a recession or stock market crash.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Reform California, a political action committee started by state Sen. Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), and legislative Republicans argue the proposal will allow Democrats to spend more money and hold on to revenue that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for deposits into a savings account to count as spending under state law.
California’s budget revenue also is vulnerable to dramatic and at times unpredictable swings from year to year based on stock market activity. Newsom has said the state should have more flexibility during times of surplus to deposit money into the reserve accounts that lawmakers could then use during deficits to prevent big cuts to social services.
Advertisement
Statewide voters originally adopted the constitutional spending limit during an antitax wave in the late 1970s. Subsequent changes weakened the measure with exemptions to the limit for different kinds of appropriations, such as spending on infrastructure, and made it easier for lawmakers to avoid exceeding the limit and triggering rebates.
Revenue last exceeded the Gann Limit in 2021 when the pandemic left California with a predicted tax surplus of about $75 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-10/gavin-newsom-new-stimulus-checks-californians-rent-assistance). As he campaigned against a failed recall, the governor set aside about $11.8 billion in cash rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election) for middle class and low-income residents under a program he called the “Golden State Stimulus.” The Newsom administration predicted a historic surplus of nearly $100 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-05-13/california-budget-surplus-swells-to-97-billion-under-newsom-new-plan) the next year.

Will Californians vote to save more tax revenue in rainy day fund?

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue.

Proposition 2, or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. 

The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. 

Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. 

California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays triggered by natural disasters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. 

“If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat.

But opponents, including most Republican lawmakers, say saving more would only embolden legislators to spend more. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue.

“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. 

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. There are no limits on what lawmakers can spend the money on.

Prop. 2 would keep those rules and allow the state to save more. Critics say state leaders have too much leeway in spending the money. 

David Crane, a former economic adviser to former Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, said the rules let “governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue. Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/), or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays (https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/el-nino-long-irs-tax-deadline-delays) triggered by natural disasters. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements) labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. “If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. Will Californians vote to save more tax revenue in rainy day fund?

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue.

Proposition 2, or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. 

The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. 

Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. 

California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays triggered by natural disasters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. 

“If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat.

But opponents, including most Republican lawmakers, say saving more would only embolden legislators to spend more. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue.

“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. 

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. There are no limits on what lawmakers can spend the money on.

Prop. 2 would keep those rules and allow the state to save more. Critics say state leaders have too much leeway in spending the money. 

David Crane, a former economic adviser to former Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, said the rules let “governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

Will Californians vote to save more tax revenue in rainy day fund?

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue.

Proposition 2, or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. 

The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. 

Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. 

California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays triggered by natural disasters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. 

“If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat.

But opponents, including most Republican lawmakers, say saving more would only embolden legislators to spend more. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue.

“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. 

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. There are no limits on what lawmakers can spend the money on.

Prop. 2 would keep those rules and allow the state to save more. Critics say state leaders have too much leeway in spending the money. 

David Crane, a former economic adviser to former Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, said the rules let “governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

The reserve fund is intended to help the state maintain essential services during economic downturns, when tax revenues may fall.
A yes vote would change how the state saves money and pays down debt, resulting in higher reserves and requiring additional debt payments for a longer period.
A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns.
No formal opposition was submitted against the measure, though some critics argue that it could limit taxpayer rebates and weaken the effect of the state's constitutional spending limit.

Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.
NO: A “no” vote opposes these changes and would keep the current rules for the state’s rainy day fund, extra debt payments, spending limit, and declarations of budget emergencies.

PROPOSITION 2
This amendment proposed by Assembly Constitutional
Amendment 20 of the 2025–2026 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type
and new provisions proposed to be added are printed in
italic type to indicate that they are new.

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO ARTICLE XVI
First—(a) This measure shall be known, and may be
cited, as the Save for California’s Future Act.
(b) The Legislature finds and declares all of the
following:
(1) California families understand that responsible
financial planning requires setting aside savings during
good times to prepare for unexpected challenges and
economic downturns. The State of California should
follow the same commonsense principle.
(2) Californians expect their government to manage
public finances responsibly, prudently, and with an eye
toward future generations. Maintaining adequate
reserves helps ensure that essential public services
remain available when they are needed most.
(3) California’s economy is among the largest and
most dynamic in the world, but it is also subject to
economic cycles, fluctuations in revenue, natural
disasters, public health emergencies, and other
unforeseen events that can place significant strain on
the state budget.
(4) When state revenues decline during economic
downturns, insufficient reserves can force difficult
choices that disrupt essential programs and services
relied upon by California families, students, seniors,
veterans, workers, and businesses.
(5) Building and maintaining strong budget reserves
during periods of economic growth helps protect
Californians from sudden reductions in essential
services and reduces the need for drastic corrective
actions during periods of fiscal stress.
(6) Sound financial planning requires looking beyond
the next fiscal year and preparing for future challenges
before they arise. Just like families save for
emergencies and unexpected expenses, California
should save during good years to protect schools,
public safety, and essential services during tough
times.
(7) Strong reserve policies promote fiscal stability,
improve public confidence in state government,
support long-term economic growth, and help preserve
California’s ability to respond effectively to
emergencies and economic downturns.
(8) Proposition 98 was enacted by the voters in 1988
to provide a minimum funding level for schools. Nothing
in this act is intended to change the calculation or
106 | Text of Proposed Laws
funding of the minimum guarantee under Section 8 of
Article XVI.
(c) It is therefore the intent of the Legislature to
strengthen the state’s commitment to responsible
budgeting, long-term financial planning, and prudent
savings by enhancing California’s budget reserves and
ensuring that the state is better prepared for future
economic challenges. Strengthening reserves is an
investment in California’s future and in future
generations.

Endorsement: Prop 2 could help California be more fiscally responsible — if our politicians bother to use it
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 15, 2026
Proposition 2 would help California stabilize its budget by requiring more money for its rainy-day reserve and setting aside more funding to pay off debts.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
What would you do if you suddenly found yourself flush with an unexpected cash windfall?
Would you run out and treat yourself to something expensive and irresponsible? Or would you pay off your debts and sock the extra money away for a rainy day?
Proposition 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (and one Republican) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20) placed on California’s November ballot, would encourage California to take the latter approach with its budget.
